title: The oldest known customer complaint is a 3,800-year-old clay tablet about bad copper

cover.alt: A small rectangular clay tablet densely covered in cuneiform wedge marks: the complaint letter to Ea-nasir.

body: Around 1750 BC, in the Mesopotamian city of Ur, a merchant named Ea-nasir sold copper ingots from Dilmun, promising they would be of fine quality. A customer called Nanni wrote him a furious letter in Akkadian cuneiform: his servant had been handed poor copper and told, in effect, to take it or leave it, and the messengers he sent to recover his deposit had been turned away rudely. The tablet, 11.6 cm tall, was dug up by Leonard Woolley’s excavation at Ur between 1922 and 1934, in ruins thought to be Ea-nasir’s own house, along with other letters complaining about his copper. Guinness World Records lists it as the oldest written customer complaint.

slides.label: tall: the whole complaint fits on a tablet smaller than a phone
slides.text: It is 5.0 cm wide and 2.6 cm thick, slightly damaged, and belongs to the British Museum.

slides.prompt: What else was found in the same ruined house?
slides.detail: One writer said he had still not received his copper; another was tired of getting bad copper. The house is thought to have been Ea-nasir’s own.

slides.question: What did Nanni say he would do with future deliveries?
options: Inspect each ingot on his own ground
slides.explanation: Nanni demanded his money back and said that from then on he would inspect the ingots one by one on his own property.

slides.heading: Why it survives
slides.text: Clay tablets harden and last where paper, parchment and papyrus rot. Letters like this one were recovered by a joint University of Pennsylvania and British Museum expedition led by Leonard Woolley, and translated in full by W. F. Leemans in 1960 and by A. Leo Oppenheim in 1967.
